newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Researchers compile Chechnya war lists before poll.
newsitem.headline: Researchers compile Chechnya war lists before poll.

text.p: Less than two weeks before elections in Chechnya, human rights researchers on Wednesday presented lists showing that more than 4,300 Russian servicemen had died in the 21-month war against separatists in the region.

The lists, laboriously compiled by the Memorial organisation, also showed that 703 soldiers were missing or held prisoner and a further 705 had been classified as "deserters". Prisoners were still held on both sides.
A Memorial researcher said it was extremely difficult to estimate the total death toll from the fighting, but he said something fewer than 50,000 people probably died.

Sergei Kovalyov, Russia's most prominent rights advocate, told a news conference the lists were drawn up after two years of cross-referencing of official data and investigations in the mountainous region on Russia's southern rim.
He called on parliament to move quickly to pass a law on an amnesty to enable negotiators to win the freedom of those still being held.

"This is a list soaked in the blood of people to whom we are indebted -- the dead, their relatives and those still alive, for whom something can still be done. It is a lesson of our sad and bloody history," Kovalyov said.

"This was a strange war to say the least, a dirty war with no legal status. It seemed to be a war and a police operation. And without strict legal norms, including a law on amnesty, it is impossible to free these fighters."

Members of Memorial, created in the Soviet Union in the late 1980s to shed light on the mass repression of the Stalin era, said conservatives in parliament were blocking the amnesty law by trying to exclude many Chechen fighters.
Kovalyov spent weeks in a Grozny bunker as the army pushed its way into the city and infuriated conservatives with his allegations of army atrocities.
He is due to visit Chechnya to monitor preparations for the January 27 presidential and parliamentary election.
The polls are the first step to restoring order in Chechnya after a treaty signed last August put an end to fighting which reduced much of the region to rubble.

Russian troops were dispatched to Chechnya in December 1994 to smash the Chechens' self-proclaimed government. They captured the capital Grozny after heavy fighting but were repeatedly beaten back in other regions by rag-tag Chechen fighters.

Russian forces have withdrawn under the peace pact and the region's legal status left in limbo for five years. Separatists view Chechen independence as a virtual fait accompli but Russian leaders say they will not accept this.
Five separatists lead the presidential race, including Shamil Basayev, denounced as a terrorist by Moscow for staging a June 1995 raid on the southern Russian town of Budennovsk.

No figures for military and civilian casualties have ever been published, although Alexander Lebed, who negotiated the peace treaty before being sacked as the Kremlin's top security official, put the figure at more than 100,000.
The report's two researchers, Olga Trusevich and Alexander Cherkasov, said the list of 4,379 dead servicemen was up to 20 percent higher than official figures.
They said drawing up lists of civilian dead and missing in the war would be much more difficult as local authorities, unlike the army, had no central registers to consult.
Many residents killed in fierce fighting had been buried hurriedly in common graves and up to 350,000 people had fled to other parts of Russia.
Cherkasov said the death toll was probably somewhere just short of 50,000, based on what he said was a realistic figure of 25,000-30,000 dead in the army's capture of Grozny alone.
